source.title: Robust LLM safeguarding via refusal feature adversarial training
source.authors: Lei Yu; Virginie Do; Karen Hambardzumyan; Nicola Cancedda

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present; no apparent garbling or truncation.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses refusal-feature ablation as a mechanistic analysis and training tool, and reports attack-alignment and defense results. It does not test toy-model superposition, feature-capacity competition, SAE feature completeness, or whether features that are superposed are one-dimensional.
record.gate_note: The paper reports mechanistic results about attack-induced shifts and a single refusal direction, recorded as adjacent findings under fits_no_version. Its ReFAT and defense-performance results do not test the listed versions of the superposition claim. Random-feature comparisons are included in the cosine-similarity analysis. Results about ReFAT hyperparameter choices are not separate rows.
record.test_reason: The study assumes a one-dimensional difference-in-means refusal direction (Arditi et al.) and uses its ablation to explain jailbreaks and to build an adversarial-training method. It does not test toy-model superposition, capacity-driven polysemanticity, SAE features, or whether features are one- or multi-dimensional. Its mechanistic results concern a single linear safety feature and attack-induced shifts.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly right. The authors say adversarial attacks share a mechanism of ablating the refusal feature. They say refusal-feature ablation approximates worst-case perturbations, and that ReFAT, which trains under this ablation, improves robustness cheaply while keeping utility. Note that restoring the feature reduces attack success, while ablating it during training gives robustness. No superposition claims are made.
record.recipe_differences: Unlike Toy Models of Superposition, this work studies instruction-tuned LLM residual-stream refusal directions and adversarial attacks, not toy networks with sparse competing features or a sparsity sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: The cosine alignment is layer-dependent and the paper notes exceptions in earliest layers. Attack type and model are varied. The authors also report ReFAT failures for prompts that induce non-English or under-represented colloquial contexts.

fits_no_version.finding: In Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct and gemma-7b-it, mean residual shifts induced by GCG, PAIR, AutoDAN and HumanJailbreaks align with the negative refusal direction, above a random-direction baseline (except early layers). Restoring the refusal-feature activation largely disables the attacks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Jailbreak attacks on instruction-tuned LLMs act largely by suppressing a single linear refusal direction in the residual stream.

fits_no_version.finding: The refusal direction from the last few layers ranks as a near worst-case perturbation of the safety score among 99 random unit-norm directions (Figure 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal-feature ablation approximates worst-case activation perturbations against LLM safety.

record.problems: The paper explicitly assumes a one-dimensional refusal feature rather than comparing one- and multi-dimensional representations. The reported cosine similarities and restoration ASRs are figure-only in the supplied text, with no exact plotted values stated in the prose. Evidence concerns three LLMs and does not directly address feature overlap, sparsity, or capacity.
record.rows_left_out: No results omitted under the 60-row limit. ReFAT and baseline-defense benchmark results were not recorded as rows because they evaluate the proposed defenses rather than measure any of the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: No toy networks, no sparsity sweep, no overlap or geometry analysis.
No neuron-level polysemanticity or capacity competition.
No measure of features spread across neurons; no dictionary or SAE recovery.

The refusal feature is assumed to be 1-D (stated as an assumption). No comparison with multi-dimensional alternatives. The ReFAT failure cases on non-English inputs are anecdotal and not framed as feature dimensionality.

record.verdict_notes: Toy Models of Superposition is cited only in support of linear feature directions. The paper explicitly assumes a 1-D linear refusal feature and does not test that assumption, so V6 is untested rather than supported. The optimality analysis (Fig. 5) has no row; it is also adjacent and not needed for any version.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, excess sparse features, overlap, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry are not tested.
Neuron polysemanticity as capacity competition, including dedicated dimensions for important features, is not tested.
Alternative causes of polysemantic neurons and whether polysemanticity indicates superposition are not tested.
The study does not measure features distributed across neurons or sparse features recovered by a dictionary or SAE.
SAE feature completeness, stability, or canonical status is not tested.
The study assumes a one-dimensional refusal feature and tests its relation to attacks; it does not test whether features involved in superposition are one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Measured layerwise cosine similarity of attack-induced representational shifts with the negative refusal-feature direction.

conditions.value: layerwise; text says except earliest layers

rows.measure: Cosine similarity; text reports average scores significantly higher than chance.
rows.baseline: Mean activation difference between two random partitions of harmful and harmless prompts (random feature direction).
rows.value: figure only
rows.uncertainty: 99% confidence intervals shown as shaded areas
rows.note: The paper describes the alignment as high and significantly above the random-feature baseline; exact values are not stated in text.

rows.subject: Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Restored the refusal-feature activation on successful adversarial prompts to the mean value for original harmful prompts.
rows.measure: Attack success rate (ASR), HarmBench classifier
rows.baseline: No RFA
rows.value: figure only; text says restoration dramatically reduces attack effectiveness
rows.uncertainty: not stated
rows.note: The paper says restoring the refusal feature effectively disables all attacks; exact rates are not stated in text.
rows.check: Restoration sets the refusal feature to the mean over original harmful prompts (Eq. 5), not harmless ones. The row's operation is correct. It is an adjacent finding only, as are r14–r24.
